style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">West Coast Community Bancorp (the &#8220;Bancorp&#8221;) is a bank holding company headquartered in Santa Cruz, California that operates through its sole, wholly owned and consolidated subsidiary, West Coast Community Bank, a California state-chartered bank (the &#8220;Bank&#8221; and together with Bancorp, are referred to in these unaudited consolidated financial statements as the &#8220;Company,&#8221; &#8220;we,&#8221; &#8220;our,&#8221; or &#8220;us&#8221;). Bancorp is subject to regulation under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, and reporting and examination requirements by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The Bank is subject to regulations and undergoes periodic examinations by the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (&#8220;DFPI&#8221;) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (&#8220;FDIC&#8221;).</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">These unaudited consolidated financial statements of the Company reflect the accounts of Bancorp and its wholly owned subsidiary, the Bank. Significant intercompany transactions and balances are eliminated in consolidation.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America (&#8220;GAAP&#8221;) requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the periods presented. Actual results could differ from those estimates. In the opinion of management, the unaudited consolidated financial statements reflect all normal recurring adjustments and accruals that are necessary for a fair presentation of the consolidated balance sheets, consolidated statements of income, consolidated statements of comprehensive income, consolidated statements of shareholders&#8217; equity and consolidated statements of cash flows for the periods presented. The results of operations for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, are not necessarily indicative of the results that may be expected for any other interim period or the full year ending December&#160;31, 2026.</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:BasisOfAccountingPolicyPolicyTextBlock" id="f-514" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Certain information and footnote disclosures normally included in financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP have been condensed or omitted pursuant to the rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission (&#8220;SEC&#8221;). These unaudited consolidated financial statements should be read in conjunction with the audited consolidated financial statements and notes thereto included in the Company&#8217;s Registration Statement on Form 10, filed with the SEC on August 31, 2026, and declared effective on September 15, 2026 (the &#8220;2026 Form 10&#8221;).</span></div></ix:nonNumeric></ix:nonNumeric><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_37"></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:NewAccountingPronouncementsAndChangesInAccountingPrinciplesTextBlock" id="f-515" continuedAt="f-515-1" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Note 2 &#8211; Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:NewAccountingPronouncementsPolicyPolicyTextBlock" id="f-516" continuedAt="f-516-1" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Accounting Standards Adopted in 2026</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In November 2025, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (&#8220;FASB&#8221;) issued Accounting Standards Update (&#8220;ASU&#8221;) 2025-08, </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Financial Instruments &#8211; Credit Losses (Topic 326) &#8211; Purchased Loans </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">(&#8220;ASU 2025-08&#8221;). The amendments in ASU 2025-08 expand the population of acquired financial assets subject to the gross-up approach in Topic 326. Under the provisions of ASU 2025-08, acquired, seasoned, non-purchased credit deteriorated (&#8220;non-PCD&#8221;) assets, such as purchased loans, are accounted for using the gross-up approach at the time of acquisition. Under this approach, an entity initially recognizes credit losses, in accordance with Topic 326, through an adjustment to the purchase price of the asset. This approach may be applied to purchased assets that are deemed to be &#8220;seasoned.&#8221; Acquired non-PCD assets are deemed seasoned if they have been purchased 90 days or more following their origination and where the acquirer was not involved in their origination. The provisions of ASU 2025-08 provide for all non-PCD loans, excluding credit card receivables, that were acquired in a business combination, to be deemed seasoned under the provisions of ASU 2025-08. The amendments in ASU 2025-08 are effective for all entities for annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2026, and interim reporting periods within those annual periods. The amendments in ASU 2025-08 should be applied prospectively to purchased financial assets that were acquired on or after the initial application date. Early adoption is permitted in an interim or annual reporting period in which financial statements have not yet been issued or made available for issuance. The Company early adopted ASU 2025-08 on January 1, 2026. The adoption of ASU 2025-08 did not have an impact on the Company&#8217;s consolidated financial statements.</span></div></ix:nonNumeric></ix:nonNumeric><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">7</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">WEST COAST COMMUNITY BANCORP</span></div><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (UNAUDITED)</span></div></div><ix:continuation id="f-516-1"><ix:continuation id="f-515-1"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Accounting Standards Issued but Not Yet Adopted </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In September 2025, the FASB issued ASU No. 2025-06, </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Intangibles &#8211; Goodwill and Other &#8211; Internal-Use Software (Subtopic 350-40) </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">(&#8220;ASU 2025-06&#8221;)</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">,</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> which provides targeted improvements to the accounting for internal-use software. The amendments in ASU 2025-06 modernize and improve the accounting for internal-use software under ASC 350-40 by removing references to prescriptive and sequential software development stages (also referred to as &#8220;project stages&#8221;) and introduce a &#8220;probable-to-complete&#8221; recognition threshold. Under ASU 2025-06, entities may begin capitalizing costs once management has authorized and committed to funding the software project and it is probable the software will be completed and used as intended. ASU 2025-06 also consolidates guidance on website development costs into ASC 350-40. The amendments in ASU 2025-06 are effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2027, including interim periods within those annual reporting periods. Early adoption is permitted. The Company is currently evaluating the provisions of ASU 2025-06 and their impact on its consolidated financial statements.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In November 2024, the FASB issued ASU No. 2024-03, </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Income Statement &#8211; Reporting Comprehensive Income &#8211; Expense Disaggregation Disclosures (Subtopic 220-40) </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">(&#8220;ASU 2024-03&#8221;)</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">, </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">which requires public companies to disclose additional information about certain expenses in the notes to the financial statements. The amendments in ASU 2024-03 are intended to enhance the transparency and usefulness of financial information by requiring entities to break down significant expense categories in the notes to the financial statements in order to address the need for more detailed disclosures about expense categories. The FASB subsequently issued ASU 2025-01 in January 2025, which clarified the effective date of ASU 2024-03. The amendments in ASU 2024-03 are effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2026, and interim periods within annual periods beginning after December 15, 2027; early adoption is permitted. The Company is currently evaluating the provisions of ASU 2024-03, but does not expect adoption to have a material impact on its consolidated financial statements.</span></div></ix:continuation></ix:continuation><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_40"></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:SignificantAccountingPoliciesTextBlock" service their debt, such as current financial condition of borrowers and guarantors, historical payment experience, credit documentation, public information and current economic trends, among other factors. We analyze all loans individually by classifying the loans according to credit risk. This analysis includes loans with an outstanding balance greater than $<ix:nonFraction unitRef="usd" contextRef="c-3" decimals="-3" name="wccb:FinancingReceivableCreditRiskMeasurementThreshold" format="ixt:num-dot-decimal" scale="0" id="f-1011">25,000</ix:nonFraction> and non-homogeneous loans, such as commercial and commercial real estate loans. The loans are evaluated and rated at the time of underwriting, at renewal, if payment becomes past due or if an event of default occurs. These risk ratings are also subject to examination by independent specialists we engage and our regulators. The risk categories are grouped into four major categories defined as follows:</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Pass</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> &#8211; A pass loan is a credit with no existing or known potential weaknesses deserving of management</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8217;</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">s close attention.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Special Mention</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> &#8211; A special mention loan has potential weaknesses that deserve management</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8217;</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">s close attention. If left uncorrected, these potential weaknesses may result in deterioration of the repayment prospects for the loan or in our credit position at some future date. Special mention loans are not adversely classified and do not expose us to sufficient risk to warrant adverse classification.</span></div></ix:continuation><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">14</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">WEST COAST COMMUNITY BANCORP</span></div><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (UNAUDITED)</span></div></div><ix:continuation id="f-912-2" continuedAt="f-912-3"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Substandard</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> &#8211; A substandard loan is inadequately protected by the current net worth and paying capacity of the borrower or the value of the collateral pledged, if any. Loans classified as substandard have a well-defined weakness or weaknesses that jeopardize the liquidation of the debt. Well-defined weaknesses include a project</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8217;</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">s lack of marketability, inadequate cash flow or collateral support, failure to complete construction on time or the project</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8217;</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">s failure to fulfill economic expectations. They are characterized by the distinct possibility that we will sustain some loss if the deficiencies are not corrected.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Doubtful</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> &#8211; Loans classified doubtful have all the weaknesses inherent in those classified as substandard with the added characteristic that the weaknesses make collection or liquidation in full, on the basis of currently known facts, conditions and values, highly questionable and improbable.</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:FinancingReceivableCreditQualityIndicatorsTableTextBlock" id="f-1012" continuedAt="f-1012-1" escape="true"><div style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Collateral Dependent Loans</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Loans are classified as collateral dependent loans when the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty, when foreclosure is probable, or substantially all repayment of the loan is expected to come from the operation of or eventual liquidation of the collateral. Collateral dependent loans are evaluated individually for purposes of determining the ACL. The ACL for each loan is measured as the amount by which the fair value of the underlying collateral, less estimated costs to sell, is less than the amortized cost of the loan. Management periodically analyzes the underlying collateral with changes in the estimated fair value of the collateral and/or estimated costs to sell reflected in the ACL for the loan. Balances deemed to be uncollectible are promptly charged-off. In cases where the loan is well secured and the estimated value of the collateral exceeds the amortized cost of the loan, no ACL is recorded.</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:AllowanceForCreditLossesOnFinancingReceivablesTableTextBlock" id="f-1530" continuedAt="f-1530-1" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The following tables present the amortized cost of collateral dependent loans as of style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Modified Loans to Borrowers Experiencing Financial Difficulty</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">At times, we adjust loan terms for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty by offering principal forgiveness, extending loan terms, deferring payments or reducing interest rates. When principal forgiveness is granted, the forgiven amount is written off against the allowance for credit losses. GAAP requires that certain types of modifications be reported, which consist of the following: (i) principal forgiveness, (ii) interest rate reduction, (iii) other-than-insignificant payment delay, (iv) term extension, or any combination of the foregoing. The Company refers to these loans as modified loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, or modified loans to troubled borrowers. The ACL for these loans is measured on a collective basis, as with other loans in the loan portfolio, unless management determines that such loans no longer possess risk characteristics similar to others in the loan portfolio. In those instances, the ACL is determined through individual evaluation.</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:TroubledDebtRestructuringsOnFinancingReceivablesTableTextBlock" September&#160;30, 2026, and December&#160;31, 2025, respectively.</span></div></ix:continuation><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_49"></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:FairValueDisclosuresTextBlock" id="f-1958" continuedAt="f-1958-1" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Note 6 &#8211; Fair Value</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:FairValueMeasurementPolicyPolicyTextBlock" id="f-1959" continuedAt="f-1959-1" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Fair value is the exchange price that would be received for an asset or paid to transfer a liability (exit price) in the principal or most advantageous market for the asset or liability in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date. We group our assets and liabilities measured at fair value into three levels based on the fair value hierarchy described in ASC 820 &#8211; </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Fair Value Measurement</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">. The fair value hierarchy gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities (Level 1 measurements) and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs (Level 3 measurements). </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are described below:</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Level 1 &#8211; Quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical assets or liabilities in active markets that the entity has the ability to access as of the measurement date.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Level 2 &#8211; Significant other observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities, quoted prices in markets that are not active or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data.</span></div></ix:nonNumeric></ix:nonNumeric><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">21</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">WEST COAST COMMUNITY BANCORP</span></div><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (UNAUDITED)</span></div></div><ix:continuation id="f-1958-1" continuedAt="f-1958-2"><ix:continuation id="f-1959-1"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Level 3 &#8211; Significant unobservable inputs that reflect a company&#8217;s own assumptions in pricing an asset or liability. Valuations are supported by minimal or no market activity for comparable assets or liabilities. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We use the following methods and significant assumptions to estimate fair value:</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Investment Securities</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">. The fair values of investment securities classified as available for sale and held to maturity are based on quoted market prices, if available (Level 1) at the reporting date. For securities where quoted prices are not available, fair values are calculated based on market prices of similar securities (Level 2), using matrix pricing. Matrix pricing is a mathematical technique commonly used to price investment securities that are not actively traded and values investment securities without relying exclusively on quoted prices for the specific securities but rather relying on the securities&#8217; relationship to other benchmark quoted securities (Level 2 inputs). For securities where quoted prices or market prices of similar securities are not available, fair values are calculated using discounted cash flows based on unobservable inputs or assumptions (Level 3).</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Loans</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">. The fair value of loans is determined as the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the rate that represents current market rates for new origination of comparable loans and includes adjustments for interest rate, credit, equity return, servicing and liquidity risk factors, resulting in a Level 3 classification. Loans are grouped according to similar characteristics such as loan type, risk classification, past due status, fixed or variable terms, repricing frequency, amortization and terms. The estimated fair values of financial instruments disclosed below follow the guidance in ASC 820 &#8211; </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Fair Value Measurement</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">, which prescribes an &#8220;exit price&#8221; approach in estimating and disclosing fair value of financial instruments.</span></div></ix:continuation><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Assets Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis</span></div><ix:nonNumeric Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 during the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Assets Measured at Fair Value on a Non-Recurring Basis</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company may be required, from time to time, to measure certain assets at fair value on a non-recurring basis. These may include assets that are measured at the lower of cost or fair value such as with individually evaluated collateral dependent loans and other real estate owned assets. The fair value for individually evaluated collateral dependent loans is measured based on the underlying collateral, which may consist of real estate properties, land, or various other assets. The fair value of individually evaluated collateral dependent loans is determined using Level 3 assumptions, and is reflective of loans for which a specific reserve has been established or where the loan has been written-down to the fair value of the underlying collateral. Generally, the Company obtains third-party appraisals to determine fair value. These appraisals may utilize a single valuation approach or a combination of approaches including comparable sales and the income approach. Adjustments may be made in the appraisal process by third-party appraisers. In determining the net realizable value of the underlying collateral, the Company then discounts the valuation of the collateral to adjust for estimated selling costs that the Company expects would be incurred in the event of foreclosure.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The fair value of other real estate owned assets is determined using Level 3 assumptions. Other real estate owned assets are recorded at fair value, less estimated costs to sell. At the date of transfer of a loan to other real estate owned status, the amount by which the loan&#8217;s carrying value exceeds the fair value of the underlying collateral, less estimated costs to sell, is recorded as a charge-off in the allowance for credit losses. As with individually evaluated collateral dependent loans, the Company obtains third-party appraisals which utilize a single valuation approach or a combination of approaches including comparable sales and the income </span></div></ix:continuation><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">23</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">WEST COAST COMMUNITY BANCORP</span></div><div style="text-align:center"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (UNAUDITED)</span></div></div><ix:continuation id="f-1958-3" continuedAt="f-1958-4"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">approach to determine the fair value of other real estate owned assets. The Company&#8217;s policy is to assess goodwill for impairment on an annual basis during the fourth quarter of each year, and more frequently if events or circumstances lead management to believe the value of goodwill may be impaired. style="margin-bottom:9pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Note 8 &#8211; Leases </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company enters into leases in the normal course of business primarily for branches, back-office operations and loan production offices. As of September&#160;30, 2026, all of the Company&#8217;s leases were classified as operating leases and have remaining terms ranging from <span style="-sec-ix-hidden:f-2175">one</span> to <ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-478" name="us-gaap:LesseeOperatingLeaseRemainingLeaseTerm" format="ixt-sec:durwordsen" id="f-2176">ten years</ix:nonNumeric>, some of which include renewal options to extend the lease for up to <ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-3" name="us-gaap:LesseeOperatingLeaseRenewalTerm" format="ixt-sec:durwordsen" id="f-2177">five years</ix:nonNumeric>. The weighted average lease term at September&#160;30, 2026, is <ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-3" name="us-gaap:OperatingLeaseWeightedAverageRemainingLeaseTerm1" format="ixt-sec:duryear" id="f-2178">7.13</ix:nonNumeric> years, and the weighted average discount rate used in the determination of lease liabilities is <ix:nonFraction unitRef="number" contextRef="c-3" decimals="4" name="us-gaap:OperatingLeaseWeightedAverageDiscountRatePercent" scale="-2" id="f-2179">3.85</ix:nonFraction>%. Our leases do not include residual value guarantees or covenants. Some leases may include a free rent period or have net operating costs associated with them.</span></div><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" name="us-gaap:LesseeLeasesPolicyTextBlock" id="f-2180" escape="true"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Leases are classified as operating or finance leases at the lease commencement date. Lease expense for operating leases and short-term leases is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Right-of-use assets represent our right to use an underlying asset for the lease term and lease liabilities represent our obligation to make future lease payments arising from the lease. Right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are recognized at the lease commencement date based on the estimated present value of future contractual required minimum lease payments over the lease term. Adjustments to the required minimum future lease payments that are variable and will not be determinable until a future period are immaterial and not included in the determination of the right of use assets and lease liabilities. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Lease extension options are included in the lease term when determining lease liabilities and right-of-use assets, when the Company believes it has an economic incentive to exercise the option. We have elected the practical expedient under </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">ASC 842 &#8211; Leases</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> to not recognize leases with original lease terms of 12 months or less (short-term leases) on our balance sheet.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We use the incremental borrowing rate at lease commencement to calculate the present value of lease payments when the rate implicit in a lease is not known. Our incremental borrowing rate is based on the FHLB amortizing advance rate, adjusted for the lease term and other factors.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Right-of-use assets are included in accrued interest receivable and other assets in the consolidated balance sheets. Lease liabilities are included in accrued interest payable and other liabilities in the consolidated balance sheets.</span></div></ix:nonNumeric><ix:nonNumeric contextRef="c-1" We qualify all our forward-looking statements by these cautionary statements.</span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_76"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Overview</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">West Coast Community Bancorp is a bank holding company headquartered in Santa Cruz, California that operates through its sole and wholly owned subsidiary, West Coast Community Bank, a California state-chartered bank. Substantially all of our business activities are conducted through the Bank. The Bank operates 10 branches across the California Central Coast, which we define as the counties of Santa Cruz, Monterey, Santa Clara, and San Luis Obispo, and primarily serves small- to medium-sized businesses, which we generally define as businesses with annual revenues of $100 million or less, service professionals and individuals. </span></div><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">32</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span><br/></span></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We offer a full complement of lending products, including commercial lines of credit and term loans, land and property development financing, commercial real estate term and asset-based loans, agricultural and farmland loans, including loans under the USDA program and small business loans guaranteed by the SBA, including 7(a) and 504 loans.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We also offer a full complement of deposit products, including demand deposit accounts, regular savings accounts, IRAs, HSAs, money market accounts and CDs, as well as fully insured deposit products offered through a reciprocal network. We provide treasury management services including electronic bill payment, a full range of mobile banking deposit services, including business mobile banking for on-the-go treasury functions, wire transfers, direct deposits, lockbox and automatic transfers, and remote deposit to electronically capture deposits from business locations. We also provide fraud prevention and card controls, enhancing security and convenience for clients. Our services also include other convenience-related services such as banking by appointment, online banking services, access to a national ATM network and banking by mail to better serve our customers.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Net interest income is the most significant contributor to our net income and is the difference between the interest and fees earned on interest-earning assets and the interest expense incurred in connection with interest-bearing liabilities. Net interest income is primarily a function of the average balances and yields of these interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. These factors are influenced by internal considerations such as product mix and risk appetite as well as external influences such as economic conditions, competition for loans and deposits, and market interest rates.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The cost of our deposits and short-term borrowings is primarily based on short-term interest rates, which are largely driven by the Federal Reserve&#8217;s actions and market competition. The yields generated by our loans and securities are typically affected by both short-term (often impacted by the Federal Reserve&#8217;s actions) and long-term interest rates, which can be driven by market expectations of future inflation, and other market dynamics. The level of net interest income is influenced by movements in such interest rates and the pace at which such movements occur.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company&#8217;s results of operations are also affected by prevailing economic conditions, competition, acquisitions, government policies, and other actions of regulatory agencies.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">On October 1, 2024, Bancorp acquired 100% of the outstanding common shares of 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp, the parent company for 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bank. With the acquisition, the Company has expanded its geographic footprint and client base. The Company&#8217;s results of operations for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 include the operating results of 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp. We may also refer to the acquisition of 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp herein as &#8220;the Merger.&#8221;</span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_79"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Critical Accounting Estimates</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We have established various accounting policies that govern the application of GAAP in the preparation of the Company&#8217;s consolidated financial statements. Certain policies require management to apply estimates and assumptions made in accordance with GAAP and involve a significant level of estimation and uncertainty, and have had or are reasonably likely to have a material effect on the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities or on the Company&#8217;s results of operations; management considers these to be critical accounting policies. The estimates and assumptions management uses are based on information available at the time, including historical experience and other factors deemed reasonable under the circumstances. Actual results may differ from those estimates, and changes in assumptions could materially affect the Company&#8217;s financial position or results of operations in future periods.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company&#8217;s critical accounting policies consist of the allowance for credit losses (&#8220;ACL&#8221;) on loans and off-balance sheet loan commitments as well as acquisition accounting. Please see </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Item 2. Financial Information &#8211; Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operation</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">s of the Company&#8217;s 2026 Form 10, for additional discussion concerning our critical accounting policies. Also, our significant accounting policies are described in </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Note 1 &#8211; Summary of Significant Accounting Policies</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> to our audited consolidated financial statements, included in the Company&#8217;s 2026 Form 10.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Pursuant to the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (the &#8220;JOBS Act&#8221;), as an emerging growth company, we can elect to opt out of the extended transition period for adopting any new or revised accounting standards. We have elected not to opt out of such extended transition period, which means that when a </span></div><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">33</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span><br/></span></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">standard is issued or revised and it has different application dates for public or private companies, we may adopt the standard on the application date for private companies. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We have elected to take advantage of the scaled disclosures and other relief under the JOBS Act, and we may take advantage of some or all of the reduced regulatory and reporting requirements that will be available to us under the JOBS Act, so long as we qualify as an emerging growth company.</span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_1844"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Non-GAAP Financial Measures</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Some of the financial measures discussed herein are non-GAAP financial measures. Generally, a non-GAAP financial measure is a numerical measure of a company&#8217;s financial performance, financial position, or cash flows that exclude (or include) amounts that are included in (or excluded from) the most directly comparable measure calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Taxable equivalent net interest income is derived by adding the tax-equivalent benefit from tax-exempt interest-earning loans and tax-exempt investment securities to total interest income and then subtracting total interest expense. The tax-equivalent benefit is derived using the federal statutory income tax rate of 21%. Taxable equivalent net interest margin is derived by dividing taxable equivalent net interest income by total interest-earning assets for the relevant period. Management considers the use of these measures to be beneficial as they allow for comparability of yields on taxable and tax-exempt assets. We believe disclosure of these measures is also consistent with standard practice within the banking industry. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Return on average tangible equity is derived by adding to GAAP net income the amortization of core deposit intangibles (less the related tax effect), and then dividing the resulting amount by average tangible equity for the period. Average tangible equity is determined by subtracting from average total shareholders&#8217; equity the average balance of intangible assets during the period, which were core deposit intangible assets and goodwill. We believe that disclosure of return on average tangible equity is beneficial as it provides an understanding of the operating results of our core business. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">These are non&#8209;GAAP financial measures that we believe provide helpful additional information for management and investors, beyond what is shown in our GAAP financial statements. However, non&#8209;GAAP measures have limitations. They should not be considered a substitute for GAAP results and may not be comparable to similar measures used by other banking companies. Other banks may use the same or similar names for non&#8209;GAAP measures but calculate them differently. As a result, caution should be used when comparing the Company&#8217;s non&#8209;GAAP measures with those of other companies.</span></div><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Results of Operations</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The following discussion of our results of operations compares the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, to the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025. The results of operations for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, are not necessarily indicative of the results of operations that may be expected for the year ending December 31, 2026.</span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_97"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%"> Net Income</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Net income for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, was $16.7 million and $43.9 million, respectively, compared to net income of $12.1 million and $36.7 million, for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025, respectively, reflecting increases of $4.7 million, or 38.8%, and $7.2 million, or 19.7%, respectively, compared to the same periods in 2025. Diluted EPS for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, were $1.59 and $4.17, respectively, compared to $1.14 and $3.45 for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025, respectively.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Net income and diluted EPS for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, increased compared to the same periods in 2025 primarily due to higher net interest income stemming from growth in average interest-earning assets, a reduction in the provision for credit losses on loans, and higher noninterest income during 2026. In addition, net income and diluted EPS for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, reflect a $920 thousand income tax benefit recorded in the third quarter of 2026 related to the purchase of $16.0 million of transferable renewable energy tax credits at a discount. The benefit increased diluted EPS by approximately $0.09 during the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026. </span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_100"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Net Interest Income</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">For the three months ended September&#160;30, 2026, net interest income totaled $37.1 million, reflecting an increase of $2.5 million, or 7.1%, from $34.6 million for the same period in 2025. Taxable-equivalent net interest income, a non-GAAP measure, totaled $37.3 million for the three months ended September&#160;30, 2026, an increase of $2.5 million, or 7.3%, from $34.8 million for the same period in 2025. The year-over-year increase in net interest income was primarily attributable to growth in interest income stemming from overall higher average interest-earning assets, including a $191.4 million increase in average loan balances. Growth in interest income was partially offset by an increase in interest expense largely associated with a $244.5 million year-over-year increase in average money market deposit balances. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The net interest margin was 5.18% for the three months ended September&#160;30, 2026, compared to 5.26% for the same period ended in 2025. The taxable equivalent net interest margin, a non-GAAP financial measure, was 5.20% for the three months ended September&#160;30, 2026, compared to 5.28% for the same period ended in 2025. The year-over-year decrease in the net interest margin and taxable-equivalent net interest margin is largely due to a decline in the taxable-equivalent yield on interest-earning assets to 6.39% from 6.54%, driven largely by a decrease in the taxable-equivalent yield on loans to 7.01% from 7.21%. The year-over-year decrease in loan yields was due in part to a $658 thousand reduction in purchase discount accretion on loans acquired from 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp and the absence of elevated prepayment penalties recognized in connection with the early payoff of certain commercial real estate loans during the third quarter of 2025. The decrease in average interest-earning asset yields was partially offset by a year-over-year decline in the cost of funds stemming from a lower overall cost of deposits in 2026, as well as the absence of interest expense associated with higher cost subordinated debentures. In the second quarter of 2026, we redeemed the remaining outstanding balance of these higher-cost debentures scheduled to mature in June 2036 and previously assumed in the merger with 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp in 2024 (&#8220;subordinated debt redemption&#8221;).</span></div><div style="text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">For the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, net interest income totaled $104.3 million, reflecting an increase of $4.5 million, or 4.6%, when compared to the same period in 2025. Taxable-equivalent net interest income totaled $104.8 million, reflecting an increase of $4.6 million, or 4.6%, when compared to the same period in 2025. The increase in net interest income was primarily attributable to higher interest income stemming from year-over-year growth in average interest-earning assets, including a $140.7 million increase in average loan balances, as well as an increase in average interest-earning cash balances of $79.9 million. The year-over-year increase in interest income was partially offset by higher interest expense on deposits due largely to growth in average money market balances, as well as an increase in interest expense on subordinated debentures which can be attributed to accelerated accretion of $1.8 million associated with the subordinated debt redemption.</span></div><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">37</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span><br/></span></div></div><div style="text-align:justify"><span><br/></span></div><div style="text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The net interest margin was 5.06% for the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, compared to 5.27% for the same period in 2025. The taxable-equivalent net interest margin, a non-GAAP financial measure, was 5.08% for the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, compared to 5.29% for the same period ended in 2025. The year-over-year decrease in the net interest margin and taxable-equivalent net interest margin was primarily due to lower yields on interest-earning assets, driven by a decrease in the average taxable-equivalent yield on loans to 6.96% from 7.16%, which is largely due to a $2.3 million reduction in purchase discount accretion on a loan acquired from 1</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp. In addition, a slight year-over-year increase in the cost of funds driven by accelerated accretion associated with the subordinated debt redemption also contributed to the decrease in the net interest margin and taxable-equivalent net interest margin. The subordinated debt redemption negatively impacted the net interest margin and taxable-equivalent net interest margin by approximately 9 basis points for the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026.</span></div><div style="text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span><br/></span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Net interest margin, as presented in the tables below, is derived by dividing net interest income by total average earning assets for the period. Taxable-equivalent net interest margin is calculated by dividing taxable equivalent net interest income by total average earning assets for the period. Fluctuations in market interest rates, as well as changes in the volume and composition of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, may materially affect both net interest income and net interest margin. Management actively monitors these measures and seeks to optimize net interest income while maintaining an acceptable level of interest rate risk through established asset and liability management policies. Interest rate risk is managed by evaluating the pricing, maturity, and repricing characteristics of all classes of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. </span></div><div id="iee38af5ba60d4130b71322a4e0c83ec1_3848290699158"></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The following tables set forth the major components of taxable-equivalent net interest income, which is a non-GAAP measure, and the related yields and rates for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026 and 2025. Factors impacting the provision include inherent risk characteristics in our loan portfolio, the level of nonperforming loans and net charge-offs, both current and historic, economic and credit conditions, the direction of the change in collateral values, and the funding probability associated with unfunded loan commitments. The provision for credit losses is recorded as a charge against current period earnings in order to maintain our allowance for credit losses, which reflects management&#8217;s best estimate of current expected credit losses in our loan portfolio at the balance sheet date.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The provision for credit losses for both loans and unfunded loan commitments was $7 thousand and $1.2 million for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, respectively, compared to $3.5 million and $5.5 million for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025, respectively. The provision for credit losses for loans for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, can be attributed to several factors including organic loan growth and changes in portfolio mix and an increase in the ACL for certain individually evaluated loans. These increases were partially offset by lower pooled reserve rates reflecting improvements in the economic forecast used in the ACL model as well as improvements in certain qualitative factors, as well as the full recovery, upon payoff, of a previously substantially charged-off loan in the amount of $1.2 million which occurred in the third quarter of 2026. The provision for credit losses was higher for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025, compared to the same periods in 2026 due largely to an increase in the specific reserve on one individually evaluated land development loan, which was based on an updated appraisal of the underlying collateral, as well as an increase in the ACL due to higher construction loan balances which carry a higher estimated reserve factor than other loans in the portfolio.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We recorded a reversal of provision for credit losses for unfunded loan commitments of $268 thousand and $371 thousand for the three and nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, compared to a reversal of provision for credit losses of $50 thousand for the three months ended September&#160;30, 2025, and a provision for credit losses of $50 thousand for the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2025.</span></div><div We invest in a variety of investment securities consistent with regulatory guidelines and internal risk management objectives, primarily to provide liquidity, taking into consideration the loan pipeline, deposit trends and other contingencies. These securities may be pledged to secure state and local agency deposits, borrowings or liquidated to generate cash proceeds. In addition, the investment portfolio plays an important role in managing interest rate risk, given that the maturity structure and rate characteristics of these assets can be adjusted in response to changes in loan and deposit composition. After meeting liquidity and interest rate risk management needs, we seek to optimize earnings balanced with credit risk exposure. Securities within the investment portfolio are classified as either AFS or HTM at the time of purchase, in accordance with applicable accounting standards.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The portfolio mix, shown in detail in the tables below, is diversified and includes securities issued by the U.S. government and its agencies, state and local municipalities, as well as smaller allocations to securities from private issuers. During the nine months ended September&#160;30, 2026, the balance of the investment portfolio decreased $13.3 million, driven by maturities, calls, principal repayments, and sales totaling $65.6 million and a decrease in the fair values of the AFS portfolio resulting from an increase in intermediate-term interest rates (5-10 years), partially offset by purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds and agency mortgage-backed securities totaling $67.4 million.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As of September&#160;30, 2026, we had $6.4 million in investment securities classified as HTM and $371.5 million in investment securities classified as AFS, compared to $6.5 million classified as HTM and $384.6 million classified as AFS, as of December&#160;31, 2025. Net unrealized losses on AFS securities totaled $23.8 million at September&#160;30, 2026, compared to $6.4 million at December&#160;31, 2025. The increase in net unrealized losses on AFS securities can be attributed to increases in interest rates during 2026. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our investment securities portfolio consists of U.S. Treasury securities, U.S. government-guaranteed mortgage-backed securities (&#8220;MBS&#8221;) and collateralized mortgage obligations (&#8220;CMO&#8221;), obligations of state and political subdivisions, Small Business Administration (&#8220;SBA&#8221;) backed securities, obligations of U.S. government-sponsored agencies, private label CMO, asset-backed securities and corporate bonds. style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Total loans held for investment were $2.34 billion at September&#160;30, 2026, compared to $2.17 billion at December&#160;31, 2025, representing an increase of $164.5 million, or 7.6%. The increase was primarily due to organic growth of lending in both legacy and newer markets, such as San Luis Obispo County. Loans made to new relationships established in 2026 had outstanding balances totaling approximately $364.6 million at September 30, 2026, with an average loan size of $1.4 million.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Commercial and industrial loans were $470.1 million at September&#160;30, 2026, compared to $369.8 million at December&#160;31, 2025, representing an increase of $100.3 million, or 27.1%. The increase in commercial and industrial loans can be attributed to organic growth in 2026 concentrated in revolving lines of credit. Commercial and industrial loans comprised 20.1% and 17.0% of the total portfolio at September&#160;30, 2026, and December&#160;31, 2025, respectively. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We have exposures to loans secured by commercial real estate (&#8220;CRE&#8221;) due to the nature of our market and the credit needs of our clients. Management and the Board manage and monitor the Bank&#8217;s CRE exposures through a comprehensive risk management framework that includes regular review of CRE concentration metrics, CRE portfolio trends, third-party credit reviews and borrower-level stress testing results, established risk-based lending standards and review of internally established concentration limits. CRE concentrations and related stress-testing results are reviewed quarterly by the Directors&#8217; Loan Committee and Board of Directors as part of the Bank&#8217;s risk management process. The Bank has adopted policies which require management to proactively monitor concentration exposures and to evaluate recommendations to the Directors&#8217; Loan Committee and Board for risk-limiting actions, including restrictive credit terms and/or participations, whenever concentrations approach or exceed 90% of approved guideline limits or when stress-testing results reflect heightened downside risk within a concentration category. Further, we typically originate CRE loans to clients within our primary market areas in which we have substantial expertise, and believe that our long-term experience in CRE lending, underwriting policies, as well as our loan and credit monitoring and administration procedures, are generally appropriate to managing our CRE concentrations.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our non-owner-occupied CRE loans have credit characteristics that differ from our owner-occupied CRE loans because repayment generally depends more directly on the income-producing capacity of the underlying property, including rental income and occupancy, rather than on the operating cash flows of a business occupying the property. As a result, the performance of these loans is more closely tied to property-level operating results, market conditions and the ability to refinance the loan.</span></div><div Our Board of Directors is ultimately responsible for ensuring policies and procedures are in place that provide for prudent management of assets and liabilities of the Bank and to ensure these policies are effectively implemented. Management establishes liquidity guidelines and reviews our ongoing compliance with the policies approved by the Board of Directors. </span></div><div style="height:45pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="padding-left:9pt;padding-right:9pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">56</span></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"/><div style="min-height:45pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span><br/></span></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The objective of liquidity management is to manage cash flow and liquidity reserves so that they are adequate to fund our operations and to meet obligations and other commitments on a timely basis and at a reasonable cost. We have developed tools to appropriately identify, measure, monitor, and control funding and liquidity risk. These tools include daily, monthly, and quarterly liquidity status reports and risk measures, cash flow projections, stress testing, and a formalized Contingency Funding Plan (&#8220;CFP&#8221;) for measuring and managing liquidity risk.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our primary sources of funds are the deposit inflows, periodic and maturity payments of principal and interest on loans, investment securities sales, maturities and paydowns, federal funds purchases, FHLB and FRB advances, other borrowings, and cash flow from operations. Our primary uses of funds are withdrawals of deposits (including maturities of certificates of deposit), loan originations, the purchase of investment securities, repayment of borrowings, dividends to common shareholders, share repurchases and operating expenses. As of September&#160;30, 2026, management believes the above-mentioned sources will provide adequate liquidity during the next twelve months for the Bank to meet its operating needs.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We seek to maintain an appropriate level of liquid assets and formal lines of credit with the FHLB, FRB and correspondent banks to ensure a safe and sound operation. Our liquid assets are comprised of unrestricted cash, short-term investments, and unpledged AFS investment securities. Our liquidity position is enhanced by our ability to raise additional funds as needed in the wholesale markets.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As of September&#160;30, 2026, total on&#8209;balance&#8209;sheet liquidity was $349.6 million, and total external contingent liquidity capacity was $1.3 billion, resulting in total available liquidity sources of $1.6 billion. As of December&#160;31, 2025, total on&#8209;balance&#8209;sheet liquidity was $457.9 million, and total external contingent liquidity capacity was $1.2 billion, resulting in total available liquidity sources of $1.6 billion. The decrease in on-balance-sheet liquidity during the first nine months of 2026 can be attributed in part to loan growth during 2026, with the deployment of excess cash into new loan originations.</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Bancorp is reliant on dividends declared and paid by the Bank and the ability to issue debt and raise capital for liquidity purposes, including with respect to cash dividends paid to shareholders. style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Capital Requirements</span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Bancorp and the Bank are subject to various regulatory capital adequacy requirements administered by banking regulatory agencies. These requirements involve quantitative measures of assets, liabilities and certain off-balance-sheet items calculated under regulatory accounting practices. Capital amounts and classifications are also subject to qualitative judgments by regulators. Failure to meet minimum capital requirements can result in mandatory and discretionary supervisory actions by regulators that could have a direct material effect on the Company&#8217;s financial statements. Management believes that as of September&#160;30, 2026, and December&#160;31, 2025, both the Bank and Bancorp met all capital adequacy requirements to which they are subject. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Bank is subject to prompt corrective action regulations. The prompt corrective action framework provides five capital classifications: &#8220;well capitalized,&#8221; &#8220;adequately capitalized,&#8221; &#8220;undercapitalized,&#8221; &#8220;significantly undercapitalized&#8221; and &#8220;critically undercapitalized.&#8221; For insured depository institutions that are adequately capitalized (and not well capitalized), regulatory approval is required to accept brokered deposits. Insured depository institutions that become undercapitalized are subject to limitations on capital distributions, as well as asset growth and expansion, and must submit capital restoration plans. See also &#8220;</span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Supervision and Regulation &#8211; The Bank &#8211; Capital Requirements&#8221; </span><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">included in the Company&#8217;s 2026 Form 10. At September&#160;30, 2026, and December&#160;31, 2025, the Bank was categorized as well capitalized under this regulatory framework. There are no conditions or events since that notification that management believes have changed the Bank&#8217;s category. </span></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><span style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Federal Reserve also sets regulatory capital requirements for bank holding companies. Because Bancorp qualifies under the Federal Reserve&#8217;s Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement, it is generally not subject to consolidated regulatory capital ratio requirements. Instead, the Federal Reserve looks through Bancorp to evaluate capital at the Bank-level capital ratios. Nevertheless, the following table shows the Bancorp&#8217;s capital ratios as if it were subject to separate capital measurements. Actual and required capital amounts and ratios are presented below for both the Bank and Bancorp as of the dates indicated: </span></div><div style="text-align:justify"><table
